kaps_punt: Weeklikse lees deur leerders: lees vir genot: Lees oor die versorging en respek vir liggaam.

items.bewering: Ouma smeer sonbrandroom op haar arms, haar nek en die punte van haar ore.
items.bron: CANSA SunSmart guidance (cansa.org.za, 'CANSA urges South Africans to be SunSmart this holiday season'; IOL 10 Dec 2025 'CANSA warns families to protect children from summer sun'): apply broad-spectrum sunscreen 20-30 minutes before going outdoors. Cancer Council / SunSmart (Australia) school resources name the back of the neck and the tops of the ears as commonly missed spots. Applying it in the morning before the match ('Die son was nog laag') fits the before-exposure advice.

items.bewering: Thandi sit haar hoed met die breë rand op
items.bron: CANSA SunSmart tips (cansa.org.za): wear hats with wide brims and avoid caps that leave the neck and ears exposed. Sydney Children's Hospitals Network (schn.health.nsw.gov.au, sun safety): broad-brimmed hats protect face, neck and ears.

items.bewering: In die eerste helfte hardloop Thandi tot haar bene warm word en haar keel droog voel. Sy drink 'n paar slukke water elke keer as die skeidsregter fluit.
items.bron: Safe Kids Worldwide sports dehydration tip sheet (safekids.org) and Children's Hospital Colorado: children should drink water regularly during play at set breaks rather than waiting until thirsty; water is the best drink for activity under an hour. A dry throat as a thirst signal and small regular sips are consistent with this. Both halves of a football match: IFAB Laws of the Game, Law 7 (theifab.com), a match is played in two equal halves, so 'die eerste helfte' is correct.
Ordinal, not a superlative claim in the risky sense. IFAB Law 7, Duration of the match (theifab.com/laws/latest/the-duration-of-the-match): a match has two equal halves, so a first half exists.

items.bewering: Anja is eerste by haar en steek haar hand na die knie uit.
items.bron: A narrative event inside the story, not an external fact. Nothing outside the story can confirm or contradict it, and it is consistent within the story: Anja was at the match from the first scene. Recorded so that every 'eerste' in the lesson appears.

items.bewering: Haar knie skuur oop, en die rou vel brand. ... "Moenie nou daaraan raak nie," sê Thandi vinnig.
items.bron: St John Ambulance UK, 'The role of the first aider' (sja.org.uk): do not touch an open wound without gloves. Keeping bare hands off a fresh graze is sound infection-control practice. That a graze stings is ordinary and uncontested.

items.bewering: "Eers my eie hande," sê die juffrou en vryf handreiniger tussen haar vingers. Sy trek dun handskoene aan en maak die sak oop.
items.bron: 'Eers' (first) checked as a sequence claim. St John Ambulance UK (sja.org.uk, role of the first aider): clean hands with soap and water or alcohol gel, then put on disposable gloves. St John New Zealand ('Infection control in first aid', stjohn.org.nz): wash hands or use sanitiser before touching a wound, then put on gloves. NHS 'How do I clean a wound?' (nhs.uk): wash and dry your hands, then put on disposable gloves if you have them. Hands first, then gloves, is the order the story gives.

items.bewering: Sy spoel die skaafplek skoon met water uit 'n vol bottel.
items.bron: NHS 'How do I clean a wound?' (nhs.uk/common-health-questions/accidents-first-aid-and-treatments/how-do-i-clean-a-wound/): 'Clean the wound by rinsing it with bottled or tap water, or by using sterile wipes.' nidirect (UK government): rinse under drinking-quality water. Rinsing a graze with clean bottled water is in line with this guidance.

items.bewering: Die juffrou druk die vel saggies droog met 'n skoon doekie. Daarna plak sy 'n pleister oor die plek
items.bron: NHS 'How do I clean a wound?' (nhs.uk): 'Pat the area dry using a gauze swab or a clean tea towel', then 'put on a sterile dressing or a plaster.' nidirect cuts and grazes: pat dry, apply a sterile adhesive dressing. The steps and their order match: rinse, pat dry, then cover.

items.bewering: Thandi sit in die skaduwee van die doelpale en drink haar bottel amper leeg.
items.bron: IFAB Laws of the Game, Law 1 (The FA's reproduction of Law 1 for 2025/26, thefa.com): goalposts and the crossbar may be no more than 12 cm wide and deep. A goal frame is a set of thin posts and one bar, so its shadow is a strip no wider than a hand. A child cannot sit in it, and it gives no real protection from the sun. CANSA SunSmart advice is to stay in the shade or under an umbrella. The story is otherwise careful about sun protection (sunscreen, a broad-brimmed hat, sunscreen put on again), so this sentence teaches the learner that a goal frame is shelter from the sun, which is false.
items.regstelling: Move her rest to real shade, the kind a child can actually sit in, such as a tree, a pavilion or a shelter beside the field. Or leave out where she sits and keep only the drinking. The same fault would also apply to any other mention of the goalposts as shade. 'Thandi byt op haar lip en kyk na die doelpale' is fine, because it says nothing about shade.

items.bewering: Haar nek is nat gesweet, en sy haal Ouma se sonbrandroom uit haar tas. Sy smeer dit weer op haar nek en op die punte van haar ore.
items.bron: Tested as a set against the morning application, 'op haar arms, haar nek en die punte van haar ore'. Putting sunscreen on again after sweating is correct: CANSA (Dec 2025 release) says reapply every two hours and after swimming, UCT HR health resource (hr.uct.ac.za) says reapply after towel drying, perspiring or swimming, and the American Academy of Dermatology (aad.org) says reapply every two hours or immediately after swimming or sweating, on all skin that clothing does not cover. But the two lists differ by exactly one item. The arms were creamed in the morning and are left out when she puts it on again, after a whole half of running in the sun. The difference suggests that you only need to put sunscreen on again where you can see sweat, or that the arms do not need it. Guidance says the opposite: sweat and time wear sunscreen off all exposed skin.
items.regstelling: When she puts sunscreen on again, it should go on all the skin that was creamed in the morning and is still in the sun, her arms as well as her neck and ear tips. Or say only that she puts the sunscreen on again, without a list of body parts that differs from the morning list. The sweat may stay as the reason she does it.

items.bewering: Sy sit haar hoed terug op haar kop en druk dit vas.
items.bron: CANSA SunSmart tips (cansa.org.za): wear a wide-brimmed hat when outdoors. This fits the earlier sentence where she puts on the broad-brimmed hat.

items.bewering: "Die pleister moet bly sit," sê Thandi ... By die huis klim sy in die bad en hou haar knie bo die water uit.
items.bron: NHS 111 Wales, 'Cuts and grazes' (111.wales.nhs.uk): keep the wound dry (waterproof dressings allow showering) and remove the dressing once the wound has closed. Keeping the plaster on and the graze out of the bath water matches this.

items.bewering: Sy was haar hande met seep tussen elke vinger en onder haar naels.
items.bron: CDC handwashing steps (as reproduced in the CDC handout at whs.mil and quoted from cdc.gov): lather the backs of your hands, between your fingers and under your nails, and scrub for at least 20 seconds. The WHO hand-washing poster (via the Mount Sinai handout) includes the spaces between the fingers. Mount Sinai and the Minnesota Department of Health list under the fingernails as a step.

items.bewering: Later borsel sy haar tande by die wasbak en klim in die bed.
items.bron: Western Cape Government, National Oral Health Month (westerncape.gov.za/gc-news/148/38209): parents should supervise brushing so that it happens twice a day with fluoride toothpaste. SA Dental Services, South Australia (dental.sa.gov.au/advice): brush at night just before bed so that the fluoride stays on the teeth overnight. A South African dentist quoted in The Citizen also says to brush every morning and every night before bed. Brushing just before bed is correct.

opsomming: Every first-aid and hygiene step in the story is correct and in the right order (clean hands, then gloves, rinse with clean bottled water, pat dry, plaster; soap between the fingers and under the nails; teeth brushed before bed), but two sun-safety details teach something false: the shade of the goalposts gives no real shade because the posts are at most 12 cm wide, and when she puts the sunscreen on again her arms are left out of a list that otherwise repeats the morning one, which suggests that only skin that is visibly sweaty needs it again.
